title: Fix a scratch in a wooden floor
intro: Scratch or gouge in your wood floor? Fill it and blend it in with wax or tinted filler.

steps.t: Clean the scratch with a damp cloth and let it dry: dirt in the groove would show through the filler.
Run a fingernail across it: if it doesn't catch, it's only in the finish; if it catches, it's into the wood.
Test the colour on a hidden spot, under furniture: match the board's tone; you can blend two sticks.
For a deep scratch, run masking tape along both sides to protect the finish.
Press the wax stick or tinted filler into the scratch, leaving it slightly proud.
Level it with the spatula held flat, pulling along the grain, and take off the excess.
steps.q: Is the filling flush with the floor, not sunken?
steps.fix: Add a little more and level it again: filler shrinks slightly as it dries.

steps.t: With filler, let it dry as the tube says, usually 30 minutes; wax needs no wait.
steps.label: Drying

steps.t: Filler only: lightly sand the patch with grit 240 until flush, without touching the board around it.
Peel off the tape and buff with a soft dry cloth until the sheen matches.
steps.q: From standing height, is the scratch hard to spot?
steps.fix: Add another thin layer, or use a darker stick to draw grain lines across it, then buff again.

tips: Light scratch in an oiled floor? Rub in a drop of the same oil with a cloth: it often vanishes.
Draw grain lines over the patch with a darker touch-up pen and the repair almost disappears.
Deep gouges across several boards or grey bare wood: the floor needs sanding; ask a floor fitter.

title: Lay a laminate floor
intro: A new floor with no glue: lay click laminate in a room over a weekend.

tools.n: Fitting kit (tapping block, pull bar, spacers)

steps.t: Leave the sealed packs lying flat in the room for 48 hours so the boards adjust to its temperature and humidity.
steps.label: Acclimatising

steps.t: Meanwhile, empty the room, take off the skirting boards and vacuum the floor.
Lay the spirit level on the floor in several places: gaps underneath shouldn't exceed [[2 mm]].
steps.q: Is the floor flat, with no big dips or bumps?
steps.fix: Fill dips with self-levelling compound and let it dry; sand or scrape down bumps.

steps.t: Roll out the underlay edge to edge, no overlaps, and tape the joins. On concrete, lay the vapour barrier first.
Measure the room width and divide by the board width: if the last row comes out under [[5 cm]], trim the first row.
Set spacers along the walls for an [[8-10 mm]] gap and lay the first row from a corner, tongue side to the wall.
steps.q: Is the first row straight and tight to the spacers?
steps.fix: If the wall is crooked, scribe its shape onto the first row and cut the boards to follow it.

steps.t: Cut the last board of the row with the jigsaw, decor face down; if the offcut is at least [[30 cm]], it starts the next row.
steps.w: Unplug the jigsaw before changing the blade and keep your fingers clear of the cutting line.

steps.t: For each new row, angle the long edge in, lower it and tap the short joint shut with the block. Stagger the joints.
steps.q: Are the end joints staggered at least [[30 cm]] row to row?
steps.fix: Take the row out and restart it with a board of a different length: lined-up joints weaken the floor.

steps.t: For the last row, lay a board on the previous one, mark the distance to the wall minus the gap and rip it lengthwise.
Fit the last row with the pull bar, tapping gently until the joints close.
Remove the spacers and fix the skirting to the wall, never to the floor, so the laminate can move.

tips: At door frames, undercut the frame with a saw resting on an offcut and slide the board underneath.
Run the boards parallel to the main window: the joints show less.
Never fix kitchen units or heavy furniture through the laminate: it has to float freely.
